reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: The most pathogenic and most drug-resistant of the rapidly growing mycobacteria, forming visible colonies within about a week on subculture
A complex of subspecies (abscessus, massiliense, and bolletii) that is ubiquitous in water and soil and a recognised cause of health-care-associated outbreaks
Causes chronic pulmonary disease, particularly in people with bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, or other structural lung disease
A leading cause of skin, soft-tissue, and post-procedural infection after cosmetic surgery, injections, tattooing, acupuncture, and catheter placement
Inducible macrolide resistance mediated by a functional erm(41) gene is common, so prolonged incubation is needed during susceptibility testing to detect it
Subspecies matters: massiliense usually has a non-functional erm(41) and responds better to macrolide-based therapy than abscessus with an active gene
Treatment is difficult, combining a macrolide (where active) with an initial intensive phase of intravenous agents, followed by a prolonged continuation phase
Surgical resection of localised pulmonary disease or debridement of infected tissue and removal of foreign material greatly improve cure rates
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium abscessus is an environmental rapidly growing mycobacterium found in natural and treated water and in soil. Pulmonary infection typically arises in hosts with impaired mucociliary clearance or structural lung damage, such as bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis, where the organism establishes chronic airway infection and granulomatous inflammation. Skin and soft-tissue disease usually follows direct inoculation through trauma, surgery, injection, or contaminated water and instruments, producing nodules, abscesses, and draining sinuses. Its intrinsic resistance to many antimicrobials, a lipid-rich cell wall, biofilm formation, and an inducible macrolide-resistance gene (erm(41)) underlie the poor response to therapy; disseminated disease occurs mainly with significant immunosuppression.
additionalDifferentials: Other rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. chelonae, M. fortuitum)
Pulmonary tuberculosis or Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease
Cystic fibrosis pulmonary exacerbation from other organisms
additionalInvestigations: Mycobacterial culture demonstrating rapid growth on solid media
Molecular identification to species and subspecies level (for example rpoB or hsp65 sequencing)
Extended drug-susceptibility testing including macrolide testing with prolonged incubation to detect inducible resistance
High-resolution CT of the chest for nodular-bronchiectatic or cavitary disease
Repeated respiratory cultures to satisfy diagnostic criteria and distinguish infection from colonisation
Biopsy and culture of skin or soft-tissue lesions with a history of recent procedures
redFlags: Rapidly progressive pulmonary disease in cystic fibrosis, with implications for lung-transplantation candidacy
Post-surgical or injection-related clusters pointing to a contaminated source needing public-health investigation
Catheter-related bloodstream infection requiring line removal
Failure to respond to macrolide therapy signalling inducible resistance
reference.prognosis: Outcomes are among the poorest of the nontuberculous mycobacteria. Pulmonary disease due to macrolide-resistant subspecies is frequently difficult to cure and may only be controlled rather than eradicated, whereas macrolide-susceptible massiliense and surgically resectable disease have better outcomes. Skin and soft-tissue infection generally responds to combined medical and surgical treatment.
pitfalls: Relying on a macrolide without testing for inducible resistance, which leads to relapse
Not identifying the organism to subspecies level, obscuring the likely macrolide response
Attempting cure with antimicrobials alone when surgery or foreign-body removal is needed
Treating a single respiratory isolate without meeting diagnostic criteria
Overlooking a contaminated water or instrument source in clustered post-procedural cases
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Confirm species and subspecies and obtain extended drug-susceptibility testing, including prolonged incubation to detect inducible erm(41)-mediated macrolide resistance, before committing to a regimen

Treat with prolonged multidrug therapy comprising an intravenous initiation phase (amikacin with tigecycline, imipenem, or cefoxitin) followed by a continuation phase, adding a macrolide such as azithromycin only where erm(41) is non-functional
Recognise that eradication is often unattainable, so aim for disease control alongside airway-clearance techniques and treatment of underlying bronchiectasis or cystic fibrosis
Pursue source control with surgical resection of localised pulmonary disease and debridement of skin or soft-tissue lesions, removing any infected catheters or foreign material
Monitor for drug toxicity, including aminoglycoside-related ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with audiometry and renal function, and track response with repeated cultures
Optimise nutrition and comorbid lung disease, including CFTR modulator therapy in eligible cystic fibrosis patients
Manage through a specialist multidisciplinary team spanning infectious diseases, respiratory or cystic fibrosis services, and surgery
